newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Analyst says Bulgaria on brink of debt default.
newsitem.headline: Analyst says Bulgaria on brink of debt default.

text.p: Bulgaria's political showdown between the ruling Socialist Party and the opposition brings closer the prospect of debt default and hyperinflation, an analyst said on Monday.

"In case there is no agreement on the currency board and the necessary preparation there is only one scenario: hyperinflation and default," said Krassen Stanchev, director of an independent think-tank, the Institute for Market Economics.

Pressure is growing on the ruling Socialist Party, composed largely of ex-communists, to hold a general election nearly two years ahead of schedule, after eight straight days of anti-government protests in the capital and provincial cities.

"The Socialists basically failed to proceed with market and structural reforms and especially with privatisation. The country may now default on its Brady debt," Stanchev said in an interview with Reuters Television.
"Now the Socialists would like a second mandate to do the opposite of what they have been doing for two years, but no one believes them now," said Stanchev.

Month-on-month inflation soared to 26.9 percent in December from just over nine percent in November after a series of price increases on basic food and fuel items. Annual inflation is running at a rate of more than 300 percent.
The lev collapsed to 670 to the dollar on Monday from 70 a year ago losing 34 pct of its value since the beginning of this year.

Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov had said last week that Bulgaria will meet $135 million coupon payments on $5.2 billion of Brady bonds due on January 28. The bonds were issued two years ago to restructure a $8.16 billion commercial debt.

The International Monetary Fund had begun talks with the outgoing Socialist government, which resigned on December 21, on the implementation of a strict fixed exchange rate regime as a last resort to stabilise the crumbling financial system.
Talks were expected to be completed after parliamentary approval for a new government, which was due by mid-January.

However President Zhelyu Zhelev postponed handing a mandate to form the government to outgoing Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, nominated by the Socialists as prime minister, until the Socialists agreed to a general election.
The IMF said it is ready to complete talks on helping to haul Bulgaria's crumbling economy back from the brink of default as soon as it has a stable government.

Stanchev said the most optimistic scenario was to have an interim cabinet and a parliament which would proceed with the draft bills which would pave the way to an agreement with the IMF and ensure debt foreign payments.
Preparations for the currency board, due to be completed by February, included restructuring the central bank, passing in parliament a viable 1997 budget and approving amendments to banking laws.
It is unclear when parliament, whose building suffered serious damage in a 10-hour demonstrators' siege on Friday, would be able to vote on the legal amendments.
The opposition has walked out of parliament until their demands for an early election are met. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
